title: The Pull Bench: How Hard Is the Outer Electron Held?
intro: Every atom has a pull on its outermost electron. You will measure that pull on eighteen atoms, find what cancels part of it, and light up a map of the whole table.
introSteps: Read the picture card: what the rings, the red nucleus and the numbers mean. That is all the reading.
Walk to the pull bench. Pick atoms from the table or drag the proton slider, then measure the pull.
Click the rings that are in the way of the outer electron and watch the protons cancel.
Halfway through, Mr. D calls a huddle. Eyes up, copy the board.
Then predict one atom, name one mystery atom, and hand in.
keyRows: Walk. On screen you move along the floor diagonals.
Use what you are facing (the pull bench).
Point at anything to see its name.

hook.ask: Sodium has 11 protons. How hard does its last electron feel them?
hook.note: Not as hard as you would think. That is what you are about to measure.

goal: Goal: find out what sets the pull on an atom's outer electron, using your own readings.

cards.body: The red circle is the nucleus and the number on it is the protons. Each ring is a shell and each dot is an electron. The outermost ring is the one that gets pulled. The pull meter on the bench shows how hard the nucleus holds that outer electron. That is all you need to start.

demo: Welcome. This tour shows every control. None of it counts toward your lab.
Walk with the arrow keys or WASD. Press E at the pull bench, the long bench with the dial and the spinning atom.
The table is your pull map. Click an atom to load it. Here is sodium.
Or drag the proton slider. Watch the atom build: each proton you add brings an electron, and new rings appear.
Press Measure the pull. The meter fills, a blue arrow tugs the outer electron, and sodium lights up on the map.
Protons alone would say 11. The meter says much less. Click the inner rings, the electrons in the way, and watch them cancel protons until your estimate matches.
Go down the column to potassium. One more ring means a longer way out, so the pull drops. Mark its rings too.
Measure a whole row. The map fills with color: darker means a stronger pull. You can see the pattern across the table.
The predict box asks sodium or magnesium before it lets you measure magnesium. The mystery atom shows rings and a pull. Count the electrons and click the atom.
That is the whole bench. Press Esc to close it. Your lab starts when the tour ends.
